item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
That is your definition of what Keter means, and clearly it is at odds with a definition of object classes that is entirely based on containment difficultly (the locked box test).

The locked box test is nothing more than a shorthand analogy for object classes, and many different "versions" of it exist. It is an oversimplification, an "in a nutshell" type of thing. I have never believed that object classes should be based entirely on containment difficulty, and even the current guidelines regarding object classes do not suggest this.

item.content:encoded:
That is your definition of what Keter means, and clearly it is at odds with a definition of object classes that is entirely based on containment difficultly (the locked box test). Many people think that object classes should have nothing to do with perceived danger. Presumably the author is using that metric, rather than yours.

Personally I like the idea that object classes are principly about containment, as it puts the emphasis of the institution's classification squarely on what appears to be their main priority.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's no guaranteed method of containment.

Not in and of itself sufficient for Keter classification.

What do you think would happen if it decided to swap places during a tense negotiation between, say, the US and N. Korea?

Highly unlikely. Keter objects require the propensity for disastrous breaches, not the potential.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I saw the discussion. While hard to contain, its containment breaches are not disastrous enough to warrant the classification. Keter objects require more than exceptionally difficult/stringent containment, their breaches must constitute an unacceptable loss of human life, or be otherwise substantially damaging. The breaches caused by this thing have the potential for severe damage, but not, from what I can see, the imminent likelihood.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Both the Keter classification and containment measures seem excessive.

The author has decided on it, and likely found reason to use said object class. As for threat to the Foundation, 'threat' is not always "the Foundation is destroyed". It could be a case of "The public knows that there is a teleporting chair and wonders what else is there out there" — a threat to the Foundation's mission statement and shift of humanity's standard for "what is normal".

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'd argue that the Keter classification includes not only danger to human life but danger to the cover of the Foundation. This is why 1548 is Keter, because it possesses knowledge of the Foundation and the ability to distribute it, even though it can't hurt anyone for several thousand years.

A threat to the Foundation's secrecy is, in a roundabout sense, a threat to the safety of mankind. And a chair that has teleported the pope poses an essential, hard to contain threat to the status of normality.

I think this thing is Keter, but only barely.

item.title: (no title)

You're wrong.

Keter-class objects are anomalies that pose an inimical threat to the safety of Foundation personnel and the rest of mankind and either require extensive and complex procedures to contain or cannot be fully contained by the Foundation's current technology and knowledge.

Both threat and difficulty of containment are considerations. Dangerous but easy to contain? Not Keter. Not dangerous but hard to contain? Also not Keter.
